title: Kepler phase tracking of 154 hump-and-spike A and F stars gives spike coherence times near 1,000 days, not the 1.5-day or 30-day spot lifetimes from autocorrelation fits
abstract: Question: the rotation 'spike' of Kepler hump-and-spike A/F stars has published lifetimes of 1.5 d and 3.6 d (Trust et al. 2020) and about 30 d (Henriksen et al. 2023), both from fits of autocorrelation-function (ACF) envelopes. Does the spike lose its phase on these time scales? Approach: for 174 published hump-and-spike stars we measured the phase of the spike in 30-day segments of the 2009-2013 Kepler light curves at one fixed frequency and calculated the correlation of the segment amplitudes against lag. In each star's own light curve we injected strictly periodic signals and signals with known lifetimes (1.5-3,000 d) as nulls and calibration. We also re-ran both ACF methods on the real data, on the data without the spike and on a synthetic strictly periodic spike. Results: of 154 stars with S/N >= 8, 133 (86%) keep more phase correlation at lags of 500-1,500 d than all 30-d-lifetime injections allow, and 146 (95%) reject 1.5 d. The fitted coherence time has a median of 959 d (quartiles 420 and 2,285 d); injections recover 300 and 1,000 d correctly. 22 spikes (14%) agree with a strictly periodic signal over 4 years. A linear frequency drift does not restore the phase of most stars, so the phase loss is mostly a slow random wander. Normal A and Am/Fm stars do not differ. The whole-light-curve ACF decay time does not change when we remove the spike (median 5.6 d with, 5.7 d without), and the band-passed ACF lifetime changes by a factor of 4.4 with the band width. No star shows a Kepler-season amplitude pattern, so the spikes are not contamination. Conclusion: the spike keeps its phase for about 1,000 d, 30 to 600 times longer than the ACF lifetimes; the ACF decay comes mostly from r modes, other variability and noise. Spike models need long-lived surface features or coherent modes. Limitations: r-mode leakage makes our coherence values lower limits; only Kepler data (4 years); we could not reproduce the published ACF numbers exactly; the test does not identify the mechanism.
